MARKET.head: Sussex wine producers band together on Rother Wine Triangle trail
MARKET.summ: The Sussex PDO is the only geographically specific accreditation in the UK below country level. English sparkling wine arguably planted its flag in the sands of the global wine industry in April 2016. At a blind tasting held at the Juveniles restaurant in Paris, a group of respected French judges rated a number of English
takeaways: Sussex winemakers are building a wine tourism initiative called Sussex Winelands, with about 150 vineyards across the county.
The Rother Wine Triangle, launched during English Wine Week, is Sussex's first official wine trail, funded by Rother District Council.
The Wines of Sussex PDO, recognised by DEFRA in July 2022, requires grapes grown within East and West Sussex and 15 months' bottle ageing for sparkling.

MARKET.head: Australian wine exports fall 7% as US loss outweighs Southeast Asia and Canada gains
MARKET.summ:
Australian wine exports declined overall in the year ending September 2026, but the results varied significantly across markets. Strong growth in Southeast Asia and Canada was offset by more challenging conditions in the United States (US). 

This Market Bulletin will analyse the latest export data, released...
takeaways: Australian wine export value fell 7% to $2.25 billion in the 12 months to September 2026, with volume down 5% to 590 million litres.
Exports to the US dropped 28% in value to $219 million, the largest drag on volume, as US wine sales and tariffs weighed.
Southeast Asia grew 16% in value to $291 million, led by Thailand, while Canada rose 12% to $185 million as American wines left shelves.

MARKET.head: Bordeaux leads fine wine trade at 39.6% share, Lafite 2005 top seller
MARKET.summ: Bordeaux led the market, claiming 39.6%, Lafite accounting for over a quarter of its trade
takeaways: Liv-ex's weekly data shows Bordeaux claiming 39.6% of traded fine wine value, with Lafite the region's top seller at over a quarter.
Burgundy fell from 24.8% to 18.4% of traded value, while Tuscany rose from 5.2% to 8.9%.
UK buyers led Super Tuscan purchases, mainly Tignanello and Tua Rita, while US buyers led Brunello buying, focusing on Fuligni and Biondi-Santi.

MARKET.head: Booze news roundup covers Uncle Nearest sale, Italian wine heist and product launches
MARKET.summ: This is VinePair’s Booze News Weekly Roundup, where we gather the hottest headlines and product releases every Friday for a snapshot of what’s happening in the beverage alcohol industry. This week, we have updates on Uncle Nearest’s potential buyers, Mark Zuckerberg’s Guinness flop, the latest product releases, and more.
takeaways: VinePair's weekly roundup reports that Uncle Nearest has potential buyers in play for the whirskey brand.
Southern Glazer's faces a bribery snafu, according to the same weekly roundup of beverage alcohol news.
The roundup also covers OpenTable's 2026 restaurant report and a batch of new product releases ahead of gifting season.

CULTURE.head: Vineyard & Winery Show returns 25 November at Kent County Showground
CULTURE.summ: New masterclass hosts, new exhibitors and, of course, stunning new home-grown wines to sample are set to make this year’s Vineyard & Winery Show another cork-popping success. With the early harvest long since safely gathered in, there can be no excuse for anyone with an interest in growing grapes, making and selling wine or simply
takeaways: The Vineyard & Winery Show, a free trade event for English and Welsh wine, runs 25 November 2026 at Kent County Showground, Detling.
About 120 exhibitors are expected, with tasting hubs featuring the 'Golden 50' medal winners and wines picked by Vineyard magazine writers.
A Pinot Noir from Biddenden, originally meant for the late Matthew Jukes, will be shown and is eligible for the new Matthew Jukes' Trophy.

CULTURE.head: Wine writer champions Ortega as versatile English grape across three Kent and Surrey wines
CULTURE.summ: I am honoured to be one of three writers, invited to contribute wine reviews of English and Welsh wines to Vineyard magazine after the untimely death of Matthew Jukes earlier this year. Though I didn’t know him well, I always admired Matthew’s professionalism, enthusiasm and sheer tasting ability. To celebrate his incredible...
takeaways: Wine critic recommends Ortega, an early-ripening German cross from 1948, as a versatile grape suited to southern England.
He highlights Biddenden's Chapter 57 (2025, £19.50), Westwell's 2025 Muscadet-style Ortega, and Denbies' botrytis-affected wine.
The columnist, one of three writers reviewing English and Welsh wines for Vineyard magazine, writes in tribute to the late Matthew Jukes.

CULTURE.head: UK vineyards pool resources through trails, joint events and wine tours
CULTURE.summ: Lucy Thomas is an independent wine tourism specialist who has visited nearly 100 English and Welsh vineyards. Here are six key take outs from her 2026 travels. Since last year’s ‘What the wine tourist saw’ article I have another 25 British vineyard and winery visits under my belt, along with eight return visits across 18
takeaways: Columnist Lucy, who has made 25 new British vineyard visits since last year, says collaboration is driving wine tourism.
Kent's 'The Kentish Wine Way' and Suffolk's wine trail group vineyards so visitors can plan multi-site trips.
Rother River Wine Tour picks visitors up at stations and shuttles them between vineyards, supported by the local council.

CULTURE.head: Real Housewives drink mass-market, sweet wines, critic argues
CULTURE.summ: What do the reality stars’ drinking habits reveal about wealth, taste, status and the economics of the U.S. wine industry?
takeaways: Cake Zine essayist, a certified wine specialist, says Real Housewives favour mass-market, high-alcohol, sweet wines, mostly Californian cabernet.
Whitney Rose on Salt Lake City's Real Housewives recommends Justin Cabernet, a roughly $22 bottle sold at Walgreens.
The essay ties the sweet-wine taste to Robert Parker's 100-point scoring system and the 'Parkerization' homogenizing of flavour.

CULTURE.head: Cloudy, unfiltered pét nat wines rise as supermarkets and restaurants embrace them
CULTURE.summ:
There’s something refreshing about unfiltered or unfined wines. We filter through a selection …

Centuries ago, Geoffrey Chaucer observed that “ther is no newe gyse that it nas old”. This truth - that there is nothing new under the sun - certainly applies to wine: every year, a well-documented or ancient viticultural...
takeaways: Marks & Spencer's Trouble organic rosé is the first cloudy still wine sold in a British supermarket.
Pét nat is bottled before fermentation finishes and usually left undisgorged, which gives it its cloudy appearance.
Zainab Majerikova, head of wine for the Ottolenghi group, says cloudiness adds texture and suits food with big flavours.

CULTURE.head: Bartenders say American drinkers abroad are curious, though they still favor vodka and Martinis
CULTURE.summ: Over decades of regular trips to Europe, Regine Rousseau, the Chicago-based founder of wine marketing and events consultancy Shall We Wine, never really subscribed to the directive often preached by U.S. travel publications: When traveling abroad, try not to let your American show. “Number one: I like wearing really bright...
takeaways: European bartenders at London's Connaught Bar and Madrid's Rosewood Villa Magna say American bar guests are curious and open.
Americans often request vodka Martinis, customized classics and US spirit substitutions, though experienced travelers increasingly try local drinks.
U.S. international travel rose about 71 percent over the past decade, and Americans took a record 24 million trips to Europe in 2025.

SCIENCE.head: MODIS satellite data validated for estimating vineyard water use in Italy
SCIENCE.summ: In North-Eastern Italy water demand for vineyards irrigation is constantly increasing, but this conflicts with the high civil and industrial rates of water consumptions in the area, which is one of the most densely populated in Europe
takeaways: University of Padova researchers used MODIS satellite data with ground weather observations to estimate evapotranspiration in a 25-hectare northeastern Italian vineyard.
Estimates were calibrated on two years of eddy-covariance measurements and independently validated on two further years, showing good consistency with in situ observations.
The authors conclude MODIS data could potentially monitor vineyard water consumption across a whole region, aiding water management in a densely populated, water-stressed area.

SCIENCE.head: Newick Wine Estate in East Sussex faces frost loss after first plantings
SCIENCE.summ: Newick Wine Estate in East Sussex is a place of outstanding tranquillity. Newick Village is situated almost equal distance from both Canterbury and Winchester, two important Cathedral cities in the south of England. It is not surprising therefore that the village has an ancient history.
takeaways: Jonathan and Charlotte Sharpe planted 37,000 vines on half of their 16-hectare East Sussex farm at Newick in 2023.
Ten frost events in 2026, four of them severe, cut the Newick Wine Estate harvest to a small tonnage, the last on 10 May.
Newick's vineyard manager Charles Negus says SWD was controlled by removing brambles and trialling Pyracantha, and GM20 Pinot Noir escaped SWD damage in 2025.

SCIENCE.head: Model simulates water and nitrogen competition in barley-intercropped Mediterranean vineyards
SCIENCE.summ: Intercropping vineyards with cover crop is a practice currently developing in wine production areas
takeaways: Researchers at Montpellier's UMR System used the APES crop simulation platform to assess competition in a barley-intercropped vineyard.
Intercropping cover crops in Mediterranean vineyards is limited by fear of water competition, while nitrogen competition has been hypothesized to explain yield drops.
The study tests water and nitrogen stress indexes for a vineyard cover-cropped with barley under Mediterranean soil and climate.

SCIENCE.head: Artelium launches Mosaic blends using PIWI varieties Divico and Cabaret Noir
SCIENCE.summ: Artelium launches Mosaic, a new collection celebrating the art of blending and the potential of piwi varieties. Artelium Wine Estate has unveiled Artelium Mosaics, a new collection of English still wines celebrating the art of blending while exploring the growing diversity of grape varieties now being cultivated in the UK.
takeaways: Artelium Wine Estate has launched Artelium Mosaics, a new range of English still wines built on blending.
The launch includes The White Mosaic 2023, The Rosé Mosaic 2025 and The Red Mosaic 2024, released at £28 RRP.
The collection introduces PIWI varieties Divico and Cabaret Noir, which the estate says suit England's climate and resist fungal disease.

SCIENCE.head: Grenache rootstock and irrigation trial shows lower water use and stomatal control
SCIENCE.summ: Under the context of global change, any decrease in water use by crops is essential, because water is becoming a more and more scarce resource, especially in Mediterranean areas, where grapevines are grown
takeaways: A three-year-old Grenache vineyard in NE Spain was grafted onto three rootstocks and grown irrigated or non-irrigated.
Non-irrigated vines had higher water use efficiency, and 110-R and 41-B outperformed 161-49 on this measure.
Stomatal conductance differences from irrigation persisted through the season, with stomata apparently kept open by water availability despite low leaf water potential.

SCIENCE.head: Italian research urges genetic and cultivation changes to meet climate and market pressures
SCIENCE.summ: In the globalization conditions possible future scenarios, optimistic and pessimistic are supposed
takeaways: A Pisa University viticulture paper argues grapevines must adapt to climate change and rising pressure on water and biodiversity.
It proposes genetic improvement and recovery of local varieties, such as Italian projects reviving native grapes, to preserve biodiversity.
The authors also report viticultural and economic trials on Lazio varieties Malvasia and Cesanese d'Affile, plus Cabernet Sauvignon, using Cordon Spur training.

SCIENCE.head: Conegliano pruning trials on Lazio grapes test yield, water and quality
SCIENCE.summ: In this work the salient results of the viticultural and ecomomic researches earned out on interesting italic varieties of Latium (Malvasia of the Lazio and Cesanese d'Affile) and an international vsriety (Cabernet sauvignon), "Cordon Spur of Conegliano" (CSC) as growing system, will be exposed
takeaways: CRA and Lazio and Padova researchers trialled Conegliano pruning systems on Malvasia, Cesanese d'Affile and Cabernet Sauvignon in Lazio.
The trials compared Vertical Tridimensional Minimal Pruning of Conegliano with and without DMRC double maturation, aiming to raise gross saleable product.
The study frames the work around vine balance, over-cropping and water scarcity under Mediterranean climate change.

SCIENCE.head: Vine balance explained: how growth and fruiting trade off across the season
SCIENCE.summ: Vine balance is a commonly used term in viticulture that expresses the concept of an appropriate balance of vegetative to reproductive growth of the vine
takeaways: Vine balance is viticulture's term for balancing vegetative growth against reproductive growth in the vine.
A balanced vine ripens its crop, sets fruitful buds for next year, and builds reserves without excessive canopy growth.
Existing indirect measures such as yield-to-pruning-weight ratio do not capture how growth balances shift during the season.

SCIENCE.head: Winter vineyard tools cut pruning labour and frost losses for growers
SCIENCE.summ: As autumn turns to winter a list of jobs looms large in the calendar. The vines need pruning and the soil needs care and attention. To make these jobs less demanding and costly, different tools can be used.
takeaways: Vineyard Magazine describes winter vineyard jobs including pruning, soil care and late spring frost protection.
Battery-powered Zanon secateurs and a tractor-mounted Provitis pre-pruner are highlighted as ways to speed up pruning.
Frost protection options named include candles, wind machines and the Ventigel, which combines heat and wind.

SCIENCE.head: Early 2026 English harvest ripens fruit fast despite spring frost losses
SCIENCE.summ: Record-early starts, ripe and healthy fruit, and a season that kept teams on their toes. Spring frost left its mark on some, but the mood across the industry is one of real excitement. As I look back to last year’s report of earliest on record, 2026 seemed in a hurry to beat it.
takeaways: Gusbourne in Kent began picking Pinot Noir on 26 August 2026, two weeks ahead of 2025.
Nyetimber in West Sussex began its earliest ever harvest on 14 September, five days ahead of the 2018 record.
Spring frosts killed emerging shoots and cut yields at some estates, including The Grange in Hampshire, while fruit quality stayed high.

SCIENCE.head: Vineyard irrigation water chemistry shapes soil nutrients and grapevine health
SCIENCE.summ: THURSDAY, OCTOBER 8, 2026. BY STAN GRANT, VITICULTURIST. Part Two of a Three-Part Vineyard Mineral Nutrient Management Lab Analysis Series.
takeaways: Nearly pure water, like Sierra Nevada snowmelt, strips minerals from sandy soils and makes them more acidic and less permeable.
Alkaline well water can be rich in calcium and magnesium, but carbonates can precipitate them and reduce their availability to vines.

SCIENCE.head: Portuguese trial tests chemical and manual thinning to cut Vinhos Verdes yields
SCIENCE.summ: Some years, climate conditions and biological events increment the fertility of vines, which can lead to over cropping and a decrease of wine quality
takeaways: A 2007 experiment in Vinhos Verdes tested chemical and manual cluster thinning on Loureiro and Borraçal vines.
Manual bunch thinning cut Borraçal yield about 41% and Loureiro yield about 26% against control vines.
Ethephon raised sugar and lowered acidity in Loureiro, while Borraçal gained no quality benefit from any treatment.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Visiting the Vineyard in the Sky
NEWSLETTERS.summ: The extraordinary story of Domaine de Beudon in Valais, Switzerland
NEWSLETTERS.author: Simon J. Woolf
takeaways: Marion Granges-Faiss runs Domaine de Beudon, a six-hectare Valais estate at 890 metres, reachable only by hike or cable car.
Jacky Granges-Faiss bought the estate in 1971; Valais's first Demeter-certified estate followed in 1992 after organic conversion in the 1980s.
Jacky died in June 2016 when a caterpillar he was using in the vineyards reversed over him; Marion has since become the de facto winemaker.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Australia’s Clare Valley: a mini-study in six wines
NEWSLETTERS.summ: The Clare Valley is an interesting region in South Australia that’s made its reputation on Riesling and Cabernet Sauvignon, as
NEWSLETTERS.author: Jamie Goode
takeaways: Wine Anorak tasted six Clare Valley wines, rating Riesling and Cabernet Sauvignon highly and Shiraz more modestly.
Grosset Polish Hill Riesling 2025 scored 94/100, with wet stone minerality and delicate citrus fruit.
Wakefield St Andrews Cabernet Sauvignon 2018, Taylors' export label, scored 94/100 for its blackcurrant fruit and earthy complexity.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Nasty Not Nice
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Why are people drinking less, when wine is better than ever? I have an idea. Wine is too good.
NEWSLETTERS.author: Tim Atkin MW
takeaways: Tim Atkin argues people are drinking less because wine is too pleasant and risk-free, and the trade is too nice.
Atkin satirically proposes insecurity-driven marketing, such as telling drinkers their wine choices make them look stupid.
He points to Riedel's glass-per-wine approach and Victorian cutlery as examples of exclusivity that could be copied.

NEWSLETTERS.head: California Cult Bubbles and More: The Latest from Ultramarine & Cruse Wine Co.
NEWSLETTERS.summ: If there were a competition for California’s geekiest winemaker, I’m sure Michael Cruse would make the final round. His willingness
NEWSLETTERS.author: Alder Yarrow
takeaways: Michael Cruse, a California winemaker, is the subject of the latest Ultramarine and Cruse Wine Co. news in Vinography.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Inside Chinon’s Lieux-Dits Project
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Vignerons lead a collective effort to recognize the vineyards behind the appellation’s Cabernet Francs
NEWSLETTERS.author: Cab Franc Chronicles
takeaways: Chinon's lieux-dits project, begun by the Chinon Syndicat in 2014, promotes named vineyard sites without an official classification or hierarchy.
Seven lieux-dits have been officially recognized so far, beginning with La Croix Boissée in Cravant-les-Côteaux in 2018.
Each recognized site receives a detailed monograph and an engraved stone marking the vineyard, with the process guided by a working group including Matthieu Baudry of Domaine Bernard Baudry.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Yet Another Vintage Port Flex Post (Tasting Selections From 1985 - 2022)
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Last week, I published a bunch of reviews from an NYC media tasting of selections from the (stellar) 2024 Port vintage. I typically follow those type of posts up with another post of other, older selections of vintage Ports that I tasted at the same event, and I offer them without much shame as simply […] This article was...
NEWSLETTERS.author: Joe Roberts
takeaways: 1WineDude published reviews from an NYC media tasting of selections from the 2024 Port vintage, which the author calls stellar.
A follow-up post covers older vintage Ports tasted at the same event, spanning 1985 to 2022 according to the title.

NEWSLETTERS.head: N is for Noirien
NEWSLETTERS.summ: What eco-geotypes tell us about grape genetics, geography, and culture
NEWSLETTERS.author: Meg Maker
takeaways: Noirien is an old French word for Pinot noir, derived from Latin niger meaning black or dark.
The Noirien group includes Pinot noir and its color mutants Pinot gris, Pinot blanc and Pinot Meunier, plus Chardonnay and Gamay noir.
The Noirien zone runs from Champagne through the Côte d'Or to Beaujolais, with its western edge reaching the central Loire.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Why Michelin Ratings Still Won’t Tell You Who Actually Made Your Burgundy Wine
NEWSLETTERS.summ: This wine guide explains why no critic's score, not even from a renowned guide like Michelin, truly reveals who made your regional wine. Consumer insight is key
NEWSLETTERS.author: Jonathan Finch
takeaways: Michelin has begun awarding one to three grapes to Burgundy wines since July, assessed on agronomy, technical mastery, identity, balance and consistency.
Julien Cruchandeau's Bouzeron Aligoté comes from old vines descended from Aubert de Villaine's massale selections, farmed under lutte raisonnée.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Telling a mountain to move
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Delving into the details of change in the DO Montsant wine region of Catalunya
NEWSLETTERS.author: Miquel Hudin
takeaways: DO Montsant has revised its bylaws to add certification for 'vi brisat', its orange-style wine, following a similar move by DO Terra Alta in 2022.
Montsant's revised bylaws also create a classification for 'minimal intervention' wines, requiring hand-harvesting, organic certification, spontaneous fermentations and low sulfur dioxide.
The author says the DO did not respond to a request for the maximum sulfur dioxide limit, which is not stated in the final bylaws posted online.

NEWSLETTERS.head: 400 Montepulciano Bottles for Thomas Jefferson circa 1805
NEWSLETTERS.summ: The wine everyone’s been gushing over since the middle ages!
NEWSLETTERS.author: Eveline Chartier
takeaways: A 1350 trade contract between the Del Pecora family and merchant Jacopo di Vanni is the oldest known document for Vino Nobile di Montepulciano, held in Florence's State Archives.
A 2024 Consorzio-unveiled document shows the term 'Vino Nobile' was first used in 1766 by the Jesuit order, not 1787 as previously thought.
In a 1806 letter, Thomas Jefferson requested 400 bottles of Montepulciano annually after receiving 473 bottles in November 1805, which he called the best he had received.
